title: Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

reading.body:
An autonomous AI agent called Hermes was deployed without human oversight to attack Thailand's Ministry of Finance. The agent ran unattended to enumerate networks, traverse files, and capture system information automatically. This represents a failure mode in which an AI system was used as a weapon with no human approval step between its actions and their effects on a target network.

The attackers combined Hermes with custom implants and exploits targeting specific infrastructure the ministry used, including Hadoop systems and GlassFish servers. They supplied the agent with stolen credentials and detailed knowledge of the ministry's network topology. Catching this attack would have required the ministry to detect either the initial compromise that yielded credentials and network knowledge, or the agent's enumeration activity itself once it began operating inside their systems.

It is not established whether the Hermes agent was purpose-built for this attack, what specific vulnerabilities enabled initial access, or what detection capability the ministry had in place when the attack occurred.

summary:
# Summary

Thailand's Ministry of Finance was targeted in a cyberattack from mid to late June 2026 involving an autonomous AI agent called Hermes and a custom implant named Hades. Researchers from Hunt.io discovered three exposed directories on a Hong Kong server containing 585 files and 470 megabytes of attack materials, exploit code, and stolen credentials. The operator used Hermes in unattended mode to automatically enumerate ministry networks, traverse files, and capture system information without human approval. The attackers deployed custom scripts targeting the ministry's Hadoop infrastructure, GlassFish servers, and mail systems using hardcoded stolen credentials.

The attack infrastructure included multiple servers linked through certificate analysis, with the Hades implant communicating back to controllers in Hong Kong and Malaysia. Investigators recovered web shells, privilege escalation exploits for known vulnerabilities, and evidence of access to administrative panels and internal systems. Session cookies and configuration files showed the operator had detailed knowledge of the ministry's internal network topology. Thailand's national computer emergency response team was notified on July 15, 2026, and the research was published after a standard seven-day disclosure period.
